edition.sessionCovered: Wed, Nov 11 (Gold breaks $4,000 to $3,987 · 10Y nears 5% at 4.98% · Iran rejects nuclear material removal · Brent $92.42 · BTC $74,100)
edition.stripNote: Thu 12 Nov. Gold broke below $4,000 for the first time in weeks on Wednesday, settling near $3,987 as the 10-year Treasury yield surged to 4.98% — within 2 basis points of the 5% threshold. CME FedWatch gives a 13.2% probability of a 50-basis-point hike at the December FOMC; Polymarket prices the 25bp at 85.5%. Oil reversed sharply higher after Iran's security chief declared Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country, undermining deal momentum — Brent rose 1.0% to $92.42 while WTI gained to $86.25. The Washington Institute counted 37 ships attacked in October through the Strait of Hormuz, the highest monthly total since the war began; two tankers caught fire from naval mines. US equities rallied: S&P 7,619 (+1.3%), Dow 52,486 (+0.5%), Nasdaq 25,466 (+1.6%), led by Apple's new record and CoreWeave's 24% post-earnings surge. Silver diverged from gold, rising 1.0% to $51.85. Base metals firmed — nickel +0.8%, zinc +1.3%. Wheat gained 1.2% to 600¢. BTC rebounded to $74,100 on a 262% volume surge. Cocoa snapped back nearly 4% toward $5,061. Uranium spot rose to $91/lb. China's Nov 10 export-control package (Announcement No. 70) officially lapsed; the Nov 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline is 15 days away. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen Nov 18–19.

overview: Gold broke below $4,000 for the first time in weeks on Wednesday as the post-CPI selloff extended into a second session. Bullion settled near $3,987 per ounce, down 1.1%, as the 10-year Treasury yield surged to 4.98% — within 2 basis points of the 5% threshold. The dollar index firmed to 102.2. CME FedWatch now gives a 13.2% probability of a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC meeting, with a 25bp move priced as near certain (Polymarket 85.5%). Silver diverged from gold, rebounding 1.0% to $51.85 as industrial demand provided support. Oil reversed sharply higher after Iran's security chief declared that Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country — a hardline stance that undercuts the nuclear dimensions of the deal framework proposed just 24 hours earlier. Brent rose 1.0% to $92.42 per barrel and WTI gained to $86.25. The Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 ships attacked in October through the Strait of Hormuz — the highest monthly total since the war began. Two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on an 'unauthorized route' through the strait. Separately, API data showed US crude inventories rose 9 million barrels in the latest week, a bearish signal that capped intraday oil gains. US equities rallied: the S&P 500 gained 1.3% to 7,619, the Dow rose 0.5% to 52,486 and the Nasdaq climbed 1.6% to 25,466, led by Apple's move to a new record high and CoreWeave's 24% post-earnings surge.

Base metals mostly firmed on Wednesday as the risk-on equity tone offset some of the dollar headwind. Copper edged up to $6.26 per pound ($13,856 per tonne LME, with the Yangshan import premium hitting a record $230 per tonne). Nickel rose 0.8% to $16,215, and zinc gained 1.3% to $3,756 on continued treatment charge tightness. Platinum and palladium rebounded from Tuesday's CPI-driven selloff, rising 1.9% and 1.9% respectively to $1,538 and $1,040. Grains were mixed: wheat gained 1.2% to 600¢ per bushel; corn held flat at 449¢; soybeans edged up to 1,230¢. Bitcoin recovered to approximately $74,100, up 0.8%, briefly touching $75,000 during the session as trading volume surged 262% — though spot ETF outflows continued for a third consecutive week at $1.18 billion. Cocoa snapped back sharply, rising nearly 4% toward $5,061 per tonne after touching multi-month lows. Uranium spot rose to approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, with FNArena reporting 'momentum up sharply.' China's November 10 export-control deadline — covering rare earth equipment, battery and graphite-anode items and five additional rare earths under Announcement No. 70 — officially lapsed with no published extension. The November 27 deadline for the gallium, germanium and antimony US-specific ban (Announcement No. 72) is now 15 days away. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, with a possible Trump–Xi meeting that could address the deadline.

watchItems.title: Gold breaks below $4,000 as Treasury yields approach 5%
watchItems.text: Gold settled near $3,987 per ounce on Wednesday, breaching the $4,000 support level for the first time in weeks as the post-CPI selloff extended. The 10-year Treasury yield surged to 4.98%, within 2 basis points of the 5% threshold — a level not seen in months. The dollar index firmed to 102.2. Kitco analysts warned of further losses toward $3,900 if yields continue rising. TD Securities sees a $3,900–$4,200 range for the near term. Central banks have bought 675 tonnes of gold year to date, up 6% from the same period in 2025, but TD says this may not offset weaker investment demand. The next key catalyst is Thursday's 30-year bond auction (prior yield 5.618%) and next week's November employment report.

watchItems.title: Iran rejects nuclear material removal — oil reverses sharply higher
watchItems.text: Iran's security chief declared on Wednesday that Tehran would not allow any enriched nuclear material to leave the country — directly contradicting a key element of the expanded deal framework proposed on Tuesday. Oil reversed higher: Brent rose 1.0% to $92.42 and WTI gained to $86.25. The Washington Institute counted 37 ships attacked in October through the Strait of Hormuz, the highest monthly total since the war began. Two tankers caught fire from naval mines on an 'unauthorized route,' and UKMTO reported a tanker struck northeast of Oman. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy blamed the tankers for travelling on an 'unauthorized route.' Middle East crude outages fell to approximately 3.8 million barrels per day, with Saudi and Iraqi output back to pre-war levels. However, Russia's refining capacity is down approximately 30% since late October due to Ukrainian drone attacks. Despite the diplomatic friction, the broader deal track — Hormuz reopening, sanctions relief, IAEA inspections — remains alive.

watchItems.title: China's Nov 10 export-control package lapses — Nov 27 deadline 15 days away
watchItems.text: China's suspension of its October 2025 export-control package (Announcement No. 70) officially lapsed on November 10 with no published extension as of that date. The package covers five additional rare earths (holmium, erbium, thulium, europium, ytterbium), the 0.1%-by-value foreign-product rule, rare-earth equipment and technology, battery and graphite-anode items, and superhard materials. The more closely watched November 27 deadline — when the US-specific ban on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials (Announcement No. 72) expires — is now 15 days away. MOFCOM's September statement referenced a January 10, 2027 political extension date but never legally amended either notice. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, with a possible Trump–Xi meeting. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing.

watchItems.title: US equities rally as tech earnings overpower yield fears
watchItems.text: The S&P 500 gained 1.3% to 7,619 on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq climbing 1.6% to 25,466 — a notably bullish equity session given that Treasury yields surged to near 5%. CoreWeave surged 24% after beating earnings expectations, while Apple hit a new record high. Dell jumped 11.9% and Arm Holdings rose 11.9%. The VIX fell 2.3% to 19.46 despite the elevated rate environment. The tech-heavy rally suggests markets may be differentiating between rate-sensitive sectors (gold, REITs) and growth beneficiaries (AI infrastructure, semiconductors). Thursday brings jobless claims, existing home sales, and the 30-year bond auction. The resilience of equities in the face of yields approaching 5% is a critical dynamic to watch.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Broke below $4,000 for first time in weeks · 10Y yield 4.98% near 5% · dollar index 102.2 · two-day CPI selloff extends
desk.sum: Gold broke below $4,000 for the first time in weeks on Wednesday, settling near $3,987 per ounce, down 1.1%, as the post-CPI selloff extended into a second session. The 10-year Treasury yield surged to 4.98% — within 2 basis points of the 5% threshold — dramatically raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. The dollar index firmed to 102.2. Gold has now fallen over 3.5% in two sessions since Tuesday's hot CPI print. Kitco analysts warned of further losses toward $3,900, with TD Securities framing the near-term range as $3,900–$4,200. Central bank buying has totalled 675 tonnes year to date, up 6% from 2025, but declining investment demand and fading safe-haven bids from US–Iran diplomacy are offsetting. The 30-year bond auction Thursday (prior yield 5.618%) is the next rates catalyst.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Diverged from gold · industrial demand provides floor · still elevated vs pre-CPI levels
desk.sum: Silver rebounded 1.0% to $51.85 per ounce on Wednesday, diverging from gold's continued selloff. The metal's dual precious-industrial profile is providing relative support: solar panel manufacturing demand remains structurally strong, and silver's industrial consumption prevents it from tracking gold's rate-driven decline in lockstep. However, silver remains well below Monday's pre-CPI levels above $53. The gold-silver ratio tightened modestly as gold fell faster. With Treasury yields near 5% and the dollar strengthening, the precious-metal complex remains under pressure, but silver's industrial floor provides a degree of insulation that gold lacks.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $86.25 · Iran rejects nuclear material removal · 37 Hormuz attacks in Oct (highest since war began) · naval mines hit tankers
desk.sum: Brent crude rose 1.0% to $92.42 per barrel on Wednesday, reversing Tuesday's slide, after Iran's security chief declared that Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country — a hardline stance that undercuts the nuclear deal framework proposed just 24 hours earlier. WTI gained to $86.25. The Washington Institute counted 37 ships attacked in October through the Strait of Hormuz, the highest monthly total since the war began. Two tankers caught fire from naval mines and UKMTO reported a tanker struck near Oman. API data showed US crude inventories rose 9 million barrels, capping intraday gains. Middle East crude outages fell to approximately 3.8 million barrels per day, with Saudi and Iraqi output back to pre-war levels. Russia's refining is down 30% from Ukrainian drone attacks. OPEC output jumped in October.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME $13,856/t · Yangshan import premium hit record $230/t · risk-on equity tone offsets dollar pressure
desk.sum: Copper edged up to $6.26 per pound ($13,856 per tonne LME 3M) on Wednesday as the risk-on equity tone offset some of the dollar headwind from elevated yields. The Yangshan copper import premium hit a record $230 per tonne, signalling strong Chinese physical demand. The LME cash price trades $175 per tonne above three-month metal, indicating backwardation. SMM reports Chinese copper stocks remain depleted at approximately 60,000 mt. The hawkish rates environment — with the 10-year near 5% — limits upside, but the fundamental supply tightness and record import premium suggest the physical market remains tight.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Holding above $135 · FOB Australia $137.50 · energy complex mixed · LNG tightness still supports
desk.sum: Newcastle coal edged up to $139 per tonne, modestly firmer, while FOB Australia thermal coal sits at approximately $137.50. The energy complex is mixed: oil rebounded on Iran's hardline nuclear stance, but LNG prices have eased from late-October highs. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping alternative fuel demand elevated. The IEA's Global Gas Security Review projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3%, the steepest annual drop on record. Coal benefits from this tightness as a baseload alternative. The 10-year yield's surge toward 5% is not directly relevant but the stronger dollar is a mild headwind.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Rebounded from CPI selloff · WPIC supply deficit supportive · PGM outperformed gold on the day
desk.sum: Platinum rebounded 1.9% to approximately $1,538 per ounce on Wednesday, recovering much of Tuesday's CPI-driven decline. The PGM complex outperformed gold as platinum's industrial demand profile — hydrogen electrolysis, auto catalysts — provided support in an equity-bullish environment. The WPIC supply deficit narrative continues to underpin the longer-term outlook. Platinum's recovery while gold fell further below $4,000 reflects the decoupling between rate-sensitive precious metals and industrial-adjacent PGMs. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Recovered from CPI selloff · EV transition headwind persists · Nornickel maintenance supports supply side
desk.sum: Palladium rose 1.9% to $1,040 per ounce on Wednesday, recouping most of Tuesday's 2% decline. The recovery was broad-based across PGMs as the equity rally and risk-on tone lifted industrial metals. Palladium's structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains the dominant longer-term dynamic. Nornickel's plant overhaul provides near-term supply support. The recovery above $1,020 reduces the immediate risk of a test of the $1,000 psychological support level, but the metal remains vulnerable to further rate-driven selling.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: 37 attacks in Oct — highest since war began · naval mines hit tankers · Iran rejects material removal · outages fall to 3.8M b/d
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz risk level remains critical with escalating shipping attacks despite ongoing diplomatic tracks. The Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 ships attacked in October — the highest monthly total since the war began. Two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on an 'unauthorized route' through the strait, and UKMTO reported a tanker struck northeast of Oman. Iran's security chief declared that Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country, undercutting the nuclear deal framework proposed on Tuesday. Middle East crude and condensate outages fell to approximately 3.8 million barrels per day, with Saudi and Iraqi output back to pre-war levels. However, LSEG Oil Research notes that normalising shipping would depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and shipowner risk appetite — even with a political deal.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Flat after Tuesday's WASDE rally · post-report consolidation · managed money still adjusting positions
desk.sum: December corn held flat at 449¢ per bushel on Wednesday, consolidating after Tuesday's 1.35% WASDE-driven rally. The bullish November WASDE — with its yield cut to 179.6 bushels per acre, below all analyst estimates — has been absorbed. Managed money is still adjusting short positions established before the report. The stronger dollar from elevated Treasury yields is a mild headwind for US grain exports. Corn's ability to hold Tuesday's gains despite the broader risk repricing is constructive. The next major catalyst is export inspection data and any updates on South American planting conditions.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Broke above 600¢ · Black Sea corridor still tight · Russian exports at half volume · Abu Dhabi grain talks in focus
desk.sum: December wheat gained 1.2% to settle at 600¢ per bushel on Wednesday, breaking above the psychologically important 600¢ level for the first time since mid-October. The move was supported by continued tightness in Black Sea export corridors, with Russian wheat exports running at about half their normal volume. Abu Dhabi talks could restart stalled grain shipments, which would be a significant bearish catalyst. The bullish WASDE-driven grains bid from Tuesday provided a supportive backdrop. Wheat outperformed corn and soybeans on the day, suggesting some position-specific buying rather than purely sympathetic movement.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: Edged higher after WASDE gains · Chinese buying still muted · South American planting underway
desk.sum: January soybeans edged up 0.4% to 1,230¢ per bushel on Wednesday, holding onto Tuesday's WASDE-driven gains. The USDA's tighter balance sheet continues to provide a supportive backdrop. Chinese buying interest remains muted, and the stronger dollar from elevated Treasury yields weighs on US export competitiveness. South American planting is underway, with early conditions generally favourable. Soybeans' modest gain reflects post-WASDE consolidation rather than fresh buying impulse. The key medium-term dynamic remains whether Chinese demand picks up heading into the first quarter.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $2,055 · briefly touched $75k · volume surged 262% · ETF outflows $1.18B third consecutive week · Fear & Greed remains in Fear
desk.sum: Bitcoin rebounded to approximately $74,100, up 0.8%, briefly touching $75,000 during Wednesday's session as 24-hour trading volume surged 262% to $31.2 billion. The bounce came despite continued spot ETF outflows of $1.18 billion — now the third consecutive week of institutional selling, with total ETF assets at approximately $95.9 billion. BlackRock's IBIT holds $60.3 billion. The Fear and Greed Index remains in 'Fear' territory. Bitcoin has closed five consecutive weeks in the red and retested support near $73,000. Ethereum traded near $2,055. The equity rally provided a supportive backdrop, but the hawkish rates environment — with the 10-year near 5% — continues to cap crypto upside.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$31 · TTF ~€83/MWh · HH $3.20 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · IEA: global LNG output to fall 3%
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) trades near $31 per MMBtu, easing from late-October highs but still up over 230% year-to-date from the low-$9s in January. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of supply offline. The IEA's Global Gas Security Review projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3% — the steepest annual drop on record — with more than 60 bcm of Qatari and UAE loadings lost from March to October. EU storage sits below the five-year average ahead of winter. Henry Hub firmed to $3.20. TTF trades near €83 per MWh. Energy Intelligence warns sustained prices near $30 could drive lasting demand substitution in price-sensitive Asian markets. Iran's hardline nuclear stance reduces near-term odds of Hormuz reopening.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · Iran hardline stance reduces near-term deal odds · Nov 27 export-control deadline 15 days
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. Iran's hardline nuclear stance — rejecting the removal of enriched material — reduces the near-term probability of Hormuz reopening, which would be needed to resume Middle Eastern sulfur shipments and ease the acute supply squeeze. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 15 days away. Until a comprehensive deal materialises, the physical sulfur market remains extremely tight.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · demand firm for 2026 · slightly softer vs recent weeks
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil eased to approximately $358 per tonne, slightly softer than recent weeks. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Potash demand remains firm through 2026. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The bullish WASDE corn report supports the demand outlook for fertilisers heading into the 2027 planting season. The broader commodity environment — with yields near 5% and a stronger dollar — is a modest headwind for potash pricing.
desk.src: World Bank · Argus Media · SP Angel

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 15 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · Nov 10 No. 70 package lapsed · APEC Nov 18–19
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical near-term catalyst remains the November 27 deadline — now 15 days away — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on antimony (and gallium, germanium, superhard materials) to the US expires. The November 10 lapse of the broader Announcement No. 70 package adds urgency. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, providing a window for Trump–Xi discussions on the deadline. Democrats' midterm sweep introduces political gridlock that could slow any bilateral agreement.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 15 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga $460/kg · Ge $4,625/kg · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not yet producing
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China (some sources report $1,800+), with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium for ex-China supply. Germanium in China sits at approximately $4,625 per kilogram. The November 27 deadline is now 15 days away. The November 10 lapse of Announcement No. 70 — covering superhard materials and rare earth technology — adds pressure to the timeline. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken its final investment decision but is not yet producing. Western supply-chain development is advancing but timelines stretch beyond 2027. China produces about 98% of global gallium.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Firmer at $5.30 vs recent $5.02 · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ supply
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) has firmed to approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, up from recent levels near $5.02. The modest recovery reflects stabilisation in steel demand rather than a structural shift. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions affect adjacent supply chains.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Snapped back from multi-month lows · ICE inventories still elevated · mid-crop could fall 42–50% · Harmattan risk ahead
desk.sum: ICE cocoa snapped back sharply on Wednesday, rising nearly 4% to $5,061 per tonne after touching multi-month lows. The rebound came on short-covering and renewed concern about the West African mid-crop outlook. Reuters projects the 2026/27 Ivory Coast mid-crop could fall 42–50% to 300,000–350,000 tonnes on irregular October rainfall linked to El Niño. Harmattan wind risk in December–January adds further supply concern. ICE warehouse inventories remain elevated at a 2.5-year high, capping the near-term recovery. StoneX projects 2026/27 global output could fall 9.6%, potentially turning the current surplus into a deficit. Cocoa's high-beta volatility underscores the thin speculative market.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: DRC quotas 96,600 t/yr · Asian market remains pressured · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds unchanged at $33,525 per tonne, under continued pressure. The Asian cobalt market is expected to remain weak through Q4 amid lackluster demand. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. The EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt intensity. The hawkish rates environment and Treasury yields near 5% add headwinds for growth-sensitive commodities.
desk.src: Trading Economics · S&P Global · SP Angel

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Near one-year low · Nov production to rise 35% MoM · supply overwhelms demand · EU caps Chinese EVs at 350k/yr
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures eased to approximately ¥90,450 per tonne, extending the decline from ¥92,000. Mysteel projects Chinese lithium carbonate production will rise 35% month-on-month in November as spodumene-based output expands. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Spodumene concentrate prices (Li₂O 6% min CIF) have fallen to $1,130 per tonne from $1,240. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. The hawkish CPI fallout and stronger dollar compound the bearish environment.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · auto demand solid
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), in a range-bound pattern. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. Oil's rebound on Wednesday modestly supports synthetic rubber costs, which indirectly benefits natural rubber. The stronger dollar post-CPI is a mild headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot surged from $86 · long-term near $99/lb · 'momentum up sharply' — FNArena · Kazatomprom Q3 +12% YoY
desk.sum: Uranium spot surged to approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, up from $86, with FNArena reporting 'momentum up sharply.' Five spot transactions were reported during the week. Long-term contract prices continue to climb, with record US contract prices near $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. Kazatomprom's September-quarter attributable production rose 12% year-on-year to 18.8 million pounds, but its average realised price of $73.51 per pound (up 17%) suggests contracts were locked at well below current spot. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver. Over 440 reactors operate worldwide with 60 or more under construction.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: China domestic NdPr oxide declining · ex-China FOB $109–121/kg · Nov 10 No. 70 package lapsed · Lynas shutdown
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, softening, while ex-China FOB prices remain elevated at $109–121 per kilogram. The lapse of China's Announcement No. 70 on November 10 — covering rare earth equipment, technology and five additional rare earths — adds further supply-chain uncertainty. Lynas' Malaysian plant is undergoing a one-month maintenance shutdown and its Kalgoorlie plant is halting for power grid upgrades, reducing ex-China output. Western buyers face premiums of up to 10x Chinese prices for heavy rare earths (dysprosium, terbium). The November 27 deadline adds further supply-chain risk.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · SP Angel

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · CIF China flat · steel demand stable
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. Ferro-manganese alloy in Europe holds at $1,045 per tonne. High-purity manganese sulfate for EV batteries is an emerging demand driver, though the lithium carbonate price decline reduces the urgency of battery chemistry diversification.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Recovered from CPI-driven dip · Indonesia 67% mine · surplus persists · risk-on equity tone supportive
desk.sum: LME nickel rose 0.8% to $16,215 per tonne on Wednesday, recovering from Tuesday's CPI-driven dip. The risk-on equity tone — with the S&P up 1.3% — provided a supportive backdrop for base metals despite the stronger dollar. Nickel's surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. Chinese smelter maintenance provides short-term tightness. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact nickel-adjacent supply chains. The 10-year yield near 5% remains a headwind for industrial metals, but the equity rally suggests the market is differentiating between rate-sensitive and growth-exposed assets.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Eased slightly · LME stocks near 4,000 mt · Myanmar ban still constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin eased slightly to approximately $46,200 per tonne, drifting lower despite the broader base metals recovery. LME inventory holds near 4,000 mt — low for the year — providing a floor. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. Tin's underperformance relative to nickel and zinc on a risk-on day may reflect profit-taking after recent outperformance. The supply-driven fundamental case remains intact, but elevated yields and a stronger dollar are capping upside across the base metals complex.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks down ~64% YTD to ~146,000 mt · smelter cuts continue · outperformed base metals
desk.sum: LME zinc rose 1.3% to $3,756 per tonne on Wednesday, outperforming the base metals complex. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments. LME inventories have fallen approximately 64% year-to-date to around 146,000 mt. The structural supply deficit continues to drive zinc higher even as other base metals face headwinds from elevated yields and a stronger dollar. The risk-on equity tone provided an additional tailwind. Zinc's outperformance reflects its tighter fundamental position relative to nickel and copper.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,725 · China FOB $1,845 · China domestic ¥550k/t · Western ~3.5x China · 15 days to Nov 27
desk.sum: European tungsten APT trades at $2,725 per mtu in Rotterdam, easing from higher levels, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu. Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels (¥550,000 per tonne). The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls on tungsten processing technology. The November 10 lapse of Announcement No. 70 — which covers superhard materials — adds uncertainty. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 15 days away. Democrats' midterm sweep further complicates the bilateral negotiating environment.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · Iran hardline stance delays Hormuz repair timeline
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. Iran's hardline nuclear stance — refusing to allow enriched material to leave the country — reduces the near-term probability of broader conflict de-escalation and delays potential repair timelines for Qatar's Ras Laffan facilities, currently estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. Commercial inventories remain at their lowest since 2008. Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · WASDE bullish for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. The bullish WASDE report — with its corn yield cut and tighter grain balance sheets — is supportive for fertiliser demand heading into the 2027 planting season. Iran's hardline stance on nuclear material reduces the near-term probability of Hormuz reopening and Middle Eastern sulfur supply resuming, which would have provided cost relief for phosphate producers.

Oil prices fell on Wednesday after Iran's security chief said Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country.
Oil ROSE on this news — Iran's hardline stance reduced deal momentum, increasing the risk premium, and Brent gained 1.0% to $92.42.
The S&P 500 rallied 1.3% to 7,619 on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq climbing 1.6% as Apple hit a new record and CoreWeave surged 24%.
The 10-year Treasury yield surged to 4.98% on Wednesday — within 2 basis points of the 5% threshold.
Silver fell 2% alongside gold on Wednesday as the post-CPI precious metals selloff continued for a second day.
Silver actually REBOUNDED 1.0% to $51.85, diverging from gold. Its industrial demand profile provided support.
The Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 ships attacked in October through the Strait of Hormuz — the highest monthly total since the war began.
US crude inventories fell 9 million barrels in the latest week, tightening supply and supporting oil prices.
Inventories ROSE 9 million barrels according to API data — a bearish signal that capped intraday oil gains.
Brent crude settled above $92 per barrel on Wednesday, up about 1% from the previous session as Iran's hardline nuclear stance raised the risk premium.
